# EnglishListing

> Find free ESL classes near you in the US, the best free online English resources, and practical guides to sounding natural when your English is already good. Independent: nobody pays to be listed. Every class listing links to an official source and shows its verification date (latest check 2026-11-13).

Key facts:
- 96 free or low-cost adult ESL programs verified in 16 US states (libraries, public adult schools, community colleges, nonprofits).
- 62 online English resources reviewed; 40 are completely free.
- Accent training guides focus on prosody (word stress, sentence stress, rhythm, intonation, linking) for advanced speakers, with a track for native Spanish speakers.

When citing, please link the specific page and mention "EnglishListing".

## Guides
- [English Pronunciation Habits Spanish Speakers Carry Over](https://englishlisting.com/guides/english-pronunciation-mistakes-spanish-speakers/): Spanish has 5 vowel sounds while English has many more, so Spanish speakers often merge pairs like ship/sheep and full/fool. Other common habits: adding an 'e' before s + consonant (eschool), giving every syllable equal length, keeping full vowels in weak words, a Spanish B/V, and D/T sounds where English uses TH. Rhythm usually matters more than any single sound.
- [How to Find Free ESL Classes Near You (US Guide)](https://englishlisting.com/guides/how-to-find-free-esl-classes-near-you/): Free English classes for adults in the US are mostly run by public adult education programs (often in public schools or community colleges), public libraries and nonprofits. The fastest ways to find one are a ZIP-code search on the National Literacy Directory, calling 211, asking your public library, and searching a local community college for 'noncredit ESL' or 'adult education'.
- [How to Learn English for Free: A Complete Plan for Adults](https://englishlisting.com/guides/how-to-learn-english-for-free/): You can learn English to a high level without paying: combine one structured free course (USA Learns, BBC Learning English or a free local class), daily listening with transcripts, regular speaking practice with real people (library conversation groups, language exchanges), spaced-repetition vocabulary, and, once you're intermediate, focused work on pronunciation and rhythm.
- [Why Your English Is Good but You Still Sound Foreign](https://englishlisting.com/guides/why-advanced-speakers-still-sound-foreign/): Most advanced learners don't sound foreign because of grammar or single sounds. They sound foreign because of prosody: which syllables and words they stress, the rhythm of their sentences, and the melody of their voice. Research on intelligibility shows prosody errors make speech harder to follow, and prosody can be trained.
- [Free English Classes Online for Adults (Live and Self-Paced)](https://englishlisting.com/guides/free-english-classes-online/): Free online English classes come in two kinds: live virtual classes with a teacher (from US libraries, adult schools, community colleges and programs like Penn's PEDAL) and self-paced courses you can start anytime (USA Learns, BBC Learning English). Many live classes are for local residents; self-paced courses are open to everyone.
- [Free English Conversation Practice Online (and Near You)](https://englishlisting.com/guides/free-english-conversation-practice-online/): The best free ways to practice English conversation are language exchanges (Tandem, HelloTalk, Conversation Exchange), free conversation circles at public libraries (many run online), local meetups, and volunteer-led conversation classes. When no partner is available, shadowing, recording yourself and talking through your day aloud keep your speaking active.
- [How to Pronounce TH in English (Think vs This), for Spanish Speakers](https://englishlisting.com/guides/how-to-pronounce-th/): English has two TH sounds: voiceless /θ/ as in think, and voiced /ð/ as in this. Both are made with the tip of the tongue lightly touching the back of the upper teeth while air flows out. Spanish speakers already have similar sounds: the Spain-Spanish z/c in cerca is close to /θ/, and the soft d in nada is close to /ð/.
- [Word Stress in English: Rules, Patterns and Practice](https://englishlisting.com/guides/word-stress-in-english/): Every English word of two or more syllables has one strong syllable: it is longer, louder, higher in pitch and has a full vowel, while unstressed syllables often reduce to a schwa. Misplacing that stress can make a correctly pronounced word unrecognizable, so it's the first thing advanced speakers should fix.
- [Best Free Podcasts to Learn American English (by Level)](https://englishlisting.com/guides/best-free-podcasts-to-learn-american-english/): Beginners should start with learner podcasts that speak slowly and publish transcripts (VOA Learning English, ELLLO, ESL Lab). Intermediate learners do well with conversational learner podcasts like All Ears English or BBC's 6 Minute English. Advanced learners get the most from native American podcasts on topics they care about, listened to actively with transcripts and shadowing.
- [How to Pronounce -ED Endings: T, D or ID (With Simple Rules)](https://englishlisting.com/guides/ed-endings-pronunciation/): The past-tense -ed ending is pronounced three ways depending on the sound before it: /ɪd/ (an extra syllable) after T or D (wanted, needed); /t/ after other voiceless sounds like p, k, s, sh, ch, f (worked, stopped); and /d/ after voiced sounds and vowels (played, called). The most common learner mistake is adding an extra syllable to every -ed word.
- [Free Citizenship Classes: Preparing for the English and Civics Test](https://englishlisting.com/guides/free-citizenship-test-english-classes/): The US naturalization test has an English part (speaking in the interview, reading 1 of 3 sentences, writing 1 of 3) and a civics part. If you filed Form N-400 on or after Oct. 20, 2025, you get up to 20 questions from a list of 128 and need 12 correct. USCIS study materials are free, and many libraries and nonprofits offer free classes.
- [Sentence Stress and Rhythm: Why English Sounds Like Music](https://englishlisting.com/guides/sentence-stress-and-rhythm/): English rhythm comes from contrast: content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) are stressed, while function words (articles, prepositions, pronouns, auxiliaries) are reduced and squeezed between the beats. Speakers of syllable-timed languages like Spanish often give every syllable equal weight, which sounds choppy to English listeners.
- [The American R Sound: A Guide for Spanish Speakers](https://englishlisting.com/guides/american-r-sound-for-spanish-speakers/): The American R is not a tap or a trill like Spanish r and rr. The tongue never touches the roof of the mouth: it pulls back and bunches up (or curls slightly), the lips round a little, and the sound flows continuously. American English is rhotic, so R after vowels (car, work, better) is pronounced too. Spanish speakers often tap it, which sounds like a D or a flap.
- [How to Improve Your Spoken English: 9 Free Methods That Work](https://englishlisting.com/guides/how-to-improve-spoken-english/): To improve spoken English you need regular speaking practice, not just study. The most effective free methods are speaking a little every day (even alone), shadowing native speakers, recording and reviewing yourself, learning phrases in chunks, practicing with conversation partners or free classes, and working on rhythm, stress and intonation so you're easier to understand.
- [Learn English Free With Your Library Card: Apps, Courses and More](https://englishlisting.com/guides/library-card-free-language-apps/): Many US public libraries give cardholders free access to tools that would otherwise cost money: language-learning apps such as Mango Languages (which includes English courses), ebooks and audiobooks through apps like Libby, and often free ESL classes and conversation groups. Getting a card is usually free for local residents; check your library's website for what it offers.
- [Schwa and Weak Forms: The Sound That Makes English Fluent](https://englishlisting.com/guides/schwa-and-weak-forms/): Schwa (ə) is the short, relaxed 'uh' sound that appears in most unstressed syllables and in the weak forms of common words like to (tə), for (fər), and (ən), can (kən) and the (thə). Using weak forms is what lets English rhythm compress; pronouncing every vowel fully is one of the clearest markers of a foreign accent.
- [American English Intonation: A Practical Guide](https://englishlisting.com/guides/american-intonation-basics/): In American English, each phrase usually has one focus word that gets the biggest pitch movement, normally the last content word or the word carrying new or contrasting information. Statements and wh-questions usually fall at the end; yes/no questions often rise. Speakers who keep a narrow pitch range can sound flat or uninterested even when their words are perfect.
- [English Vowels for Spanish Speakers: Minimal Pairs That Matter](https://englishlisting.com/guides/english-vowels-for-spanish-speakers-minimal-pairs/): Spanish has five vowel sounds; General American English has around a dozen plus diphthongs. Spanish speakers tend to map several English vowels onto one Spanish vowel, so pairs like ship/sheep, full/fool, cat/cut/cot and bed/bad sound the same. The fix is to learn the contrasts one at a time with minimal pairs, paying attention to tongue position, tension and length.
- [What Is Adult Basic Education (ABE)? Free Adult Education Classes Explained](https://englishlisting.com/guides/what-is-adult-basic-education-abe/): Adult education in the US is a network of mostly free or low-cost programs for adults 16 and older, run by school districts, colleges, libraries and nonprofits. It usually includes Adult Basic Education (ABE: reading, writing and math), English as a Second Language (ESL), high school equivalency prep (GED or HiSET) and job training. Many get federal funding under WIOA Title II.
- [Linking and Connected Speech in American English](https://englishlisting.com/guides/linking-and-connected-speech/): Native speakers don't pronounce words one by one; they join them into phrases. The main processes are consonant-to-vowel linking (an apple → a-napple), the American flap T (water → wader), dropping or softening sounds between consonants (next day → nex day), and sounds blending into each other (did you → didja). Learning them improves both listening and fluency.
- [Spanish–English False Friends: 30 Words That Trick Spanish Speakers](https://englishlisting.com/guides/spanish-english-false-friends/): False friends are words that look or sound similar in two languages but have different meanings. For Spanish speakers, the most common traps include embarrassed (avergonzado, not embarazada), actually (en realidad, not actualmente), library (biblioteca, not librería), sensible (sensato, not sensible) and assist (ayudar, not asistir).
- [The Shadowing Technique: How to Do It Right (Free Tools)](https://englishlisting.com/guides/shadowing-technique/): Shadowing is repeating a native recording almost simultaneously, copying its rhythm, stress and melody. Done with short clips, a transcript and recordings of yourself, it trains prosody and listening together. Classroom research on shadowing reports benefits mainly for listening comprehension, and it is a direct way to practice the prosody that affects how easily you're understood.
- [Thought Groups and Pausing: How to Sound Clear in English](https://englishlisting.com/guides/thought-groups-and-pausing/): A thought group is a short chunk of words that forms one idea, said as a unit with one main stressed word and usually followed by a small pause. Dividing long sentences into thought groups, instead of pausing randomly or not at all, makes your English much easier to follow, even with an accent.
- [How to Sound More Confident in English Meetings](https://englishlisting.com/guides/how-to-sound-more-confident-in-english-meetings/): Sounding confident in English meetings is mostly about delivery, not vocabulary. Finish statements with falling intonation, cut extra hedges and fillers, pause between ideas instead of rushing, stress the key word in each phrase, and prepare a few ready-made phrases for interrupting, disagreeing and asking for clarification.
